title: Live-In Relationships and the Law in India: Maintenance, Protection and What Actually Qualifies
meta_description: What Indian law actually protects in a live-in relationship, who qualifies for maintenance, and why registration rules are now emerging in some states.
intro: A woman walks into the office after a long relationship ends, no marriage certificate, often no joint lease even, asking whether she has any rights at all. The honest answer is that Indian law does recognise rights arising out of a live-in relationship, but it is built on a fairly specific set of conditions, and a casual or short-lived arrangement will not automatically qualify just because the couple lived under one roof for a while.

This guide sets out what Indian courts have actually required before extending protection and maintenance to a live-in partner, where the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 fits in, and a notable state-level shift toward requiring registration of these relationships that practitioners should be tracking.

sections.heading: What has to be shown before a live-in relationship gets legal protection
paragraphs: The Supreme Court's decisions in D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal and Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma remain the reference point for what qualifies. The core requirement is that the relationship resemble a marriage in substance, meaning the couple held themselves out to society as being akin to spouses, were of legal age to marry, were otherwise qualified to enter a legal marriage including being unmarried to anyone else at the time, and voluntarily cohabited for a significant period, not a fleeting or casual arrangement. A relationship that fails this test, such as a short term or purely casual association, or one involving a party who was at the time validly married to someone else, generally falls outside the protection these rulings extend.

This distinction matters a great deal in practice, because a partner who was in what amounted to an adulterous relationship, where one party remained married to a third person throughout, has in some reported decisions been treated differently and denied the same protection as a partner in a genuine marriage-like relationship between two otherwise unmarried people. Courts examine the actual conduct of the couple rather than a single factor, looking at matters such as the duration of the relationship, whether they shared a household and finances, whether they presented as a couple to family and community, and whether there were children from the relationship, as indicators of whether the relationship genuinely resembled a marriage rather than a temporary or purely physical arrangement.

sections.heading: Maintenance and the route through the Domestic Violence Act
paragraphs: The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 is the primary statutory route for a woman in a qualifying live-in relationship, because Section 2(f) of the Act defines a domestic relationship broadly enough to cover a relationship in the nature of marriage, beyond a formally solemnised one. Once a relationship is found to fall within that definition, the aggrieved woman can seek the full range of reliefs the Act provides, including a protection order against further violence, a residence order preserving her right to stay in the shared household, and monetary relief covering maintenance, medical expenses and loss of earnings, through a comparatively quick summary procedure before a Magistrate rather than a full blown civil suit.

Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, which provides for maintenance for a wife, has also been read by courts in appropriate cases to extend to a woman in a marriage-like relationship, treating the word wife in a purposive rather than a strictly literal sense where the underlying relationship meets the marriage-like threshold described above. A woman pursuing maintenance should generally consider both routes, since the Domestic Violence Act offers a wider basket of reliefs including residence and protection orders, while a Section 125 application focuses specifically on maintenance and can sometimes move through a more familiar procedural track depending on the forum.

sections.heading: Children born of a live-in relationship
paragraphs: Courts have been considerably more consistent and protective on this point than on the adult partners' own rights against each other. A child born of a live-in relationship that meets the marriage-like threshold, or even one that does not fully meet it, is generally treated as a legitimate child for purposes of maintenance and inheritance, on the broader constitutional principle that a child should not be made to suffer for the circumstances of their parents' relationship. This line of reasoning draws on the presumption of marriage that arises from prolonged cohabitation, traceable to the Supreme Court's older ruling in Badri Prasad v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, which treated long cohabitation as giving rise to a presumption, rebuttable on contrary proof, that the couple were validly married.

Practitioners advising a client on a live-in separation involving children should treat the child's maintenance and inheritance claims as largely insulated from the more contested question of whether the adult partners' own relationship satisfies the marriage-like test, since the child's rights do not depend on resolving that question in the parents' favour.

sections.heading: The emerging registration requirement
paragraphs: A genuinely new development worth tracking is the move toward formal registration of live-in relationships at the state level. Uttarakhand's Uniform Civil Code, which came into force in 2024 and 2025, requires live-in couples in the state to register their relationship with the designated authority, with penalties contemplated for non-compliance, marking a significant departure from the earlier position where live-in relationships existed entirely outside any registration framework. A Rajasthan High Court ruling in January 2025 has separately touched on registration of live-in relationships with the competent authority, suggesting the judicial trend in at least some states is moving toward treating registration as a meaningful, expected step rather than an optional formality.

For couples and practitioners outside Uttarakhand, this is not yet a uniform national requirement, and the position varies by state, but the direction of travel is clear enough that a client contemplating a long term live-in arrangement should be advised to check the specific state's current position rather than assume no registration framework applies anywhere.

sections.heading: Practical advice for someone in, or leaving, a live-in relationship
paragraphs: A partner wanting to strengthen their position, whether to secure maintenance later or simply to have clarity during the relationship, should keep documentary evidence of the relationship's marriage-like character as it develops rather than trying to reconstruct it after a dispute arises: joint bank accounts or financial contributions, a shared lease or utility bills in both names, photographs and communications showing the relationship was presented to family and friends as akin to marriage, and any documents relating to children if applicable.

On separation, a woman considering her options should move promptly, both because delay can weaken an otherwise strong claim and because certain reliefs under the Domestic Violence Act, such as a residence order protecting continued occupation of a shared household, are far easier to secure while the parties are still in effective control of that household than after one partner has already been excluded from it. Where the relationship clearly meets the marriage-like threshold, filing under the Domestic Violence Act alongside, or instead of, a Section 125 application is usually the more complete route given the wider basket of reliefs it offers.

faqs.q: We lived together for eight months before splitting up. Do I have any maintenance claim?
faqs.a: Possibly not, if the relationship was relatively brief and did not otherwise display the features of a marriage-like relationship, such as being held out to society as a couple and significant shared domestic life. Courts have required the relationship to be stable and marriage-like, not a short term or casual arrangement, before extending maintenance protection.

faqs.q: My partner was still legally married to someone else throughout our relationship. Can I still claim protection as a live-in partner?
faqs.a: This is genuinely contested territory. Some reported decisions have denied the same protection where one partner remained validly married to a third person throughout, treating the arrangement as outside the marriage-like test, while the specific facts of your relationship could still matter. Get specific advice before assuming either outcome.

faqs.q: We have a child together but were never married. Does our child have inheritance rights?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Courts have consistently protected the rights of children born of live-in relationships, treating them as entitled to maintenance and inheritance on the principle that a child should not bear the consequences of the parents' relationship status, often supported by the presumption of marriage arising from prolonged cohabitation.

faqs.q: Do I need to register my live-in relationship somewhere?
faqs.a: It depends on the state. Uttarakhand's Uniform Civil Code now requires registration of live-in relationships with penalties for non-compliance, and some other states are moving in a similar direction following recent High Court rulings. There is no single uniform national registration requirement yet, so check your specific state's current position.

verification_notes: Confirmed the D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal and Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma marriage-like relationship test, including the requirement that both parties be otherwise qualified to marry and the treatment of relationships involving a party already validly married to a third person, from LiveLaw's analytical article and SCC Online Blog's February 2026 piece on women's rights in live-in relationships, which both consistently describe this framework. Confirmed the Domestic Violence Act's Section 2(f) coverage of marriage-like relationships and the availability of protection, residence and monetary relief orders, and the Section 125 CrPC maintenance route being read to extend to marriage-like relationships in appropriate cases, from the same sources along with Legally India's commentary. Confirmed the Badri Prasad presumption of marriage from prolonged cohabitation and its use in protecting children's inheritance and maintenance rights from multiple law-firm commentary sources describing it consistently. Confirmed Uttarakhand's Uniform Civil Code registration requirement for live-in relationships and the Rajasthan High Court's January 2025 ruling touching on registration from secondary legal commentary (Legal Vidhiya and related sources), though the Rajasthan ruling's precise holding was not independently verified against the judgment text and is accordingly described in general terms as 'touching on' registration rather than stating a specific operative holding. Left out: a specific, confirmed 2024-2026 Supreme Court ruling directly reiterating or modifying the Velusamy/Indra Sarma test, since none was found in the searches conducted; the guide relies on the settled Supreme Court precedent from 2010 and 2013 together with the more recent state-level registration developments instead.
